entry.dc:title: Protection of thermal springs in a region of brown-coal opencast mining
entry.dc:creator: Skorepova J.
entry.dc:description: The experimental modelling method is dealt with, which is used for prediction of deformations and possibilities of outflows occurring at the bottom of an open-pit mine during the excavation of brown coal. Thermal gas-bearing artesian water exerts an uplift pressure on the impervious subsoil of the coal seam and threatens the stability of the mine bottom. The breakthrough of the mine bottom would seriously affect the groundwater regime within the wide neighbourhood. Due to the fact that the mining is carried out within the protection zone of spa springs, these might be endangered by mining activities. (Author)

entry.dc:title: Digging in
entry.dc:creator: ANON
entry.dc:description: Ground engineering works required during the improvement of the A55 North Wales Coast Road, U.K., are described. These included piling through soft alluvial material, crossing disused lead mines, negotiating opencast mining works and installing retaining walls and barette foundations. Details of the methods adopted and construction difficulties encountered are included. (D.W.Taylor)

entry.dc:title: Early-diagenetic deformation structures in the overburden of the bełchatw brown-coal mine (central poland): A predictive tool regarding engineering-geological conditions during exploitation
entry.dc:creator: Van Loon A.J.
entry.dc:description: This chapter focuses on the early-diagenetic deformation structures in the overburden of the belchatów brown-coal mine. Optimization of open-cast mining, including removal of the overburden, requires good planning that should be based on reliable prediction of the working conditions. Investigations made in this framework, in connection with opencast mining of unconsolidated sediments, tend to focus on the characteristics of the sediments with respect to: (1) their workability by mining equipment (excavators, conveyor belts, etc.), (2) the dewatering of the material, and (3) the stability of the mine's slopes. Such analyses are traditionally based on lithology, the vertical succession of layers with different lithology, and the physical mechanical parameters of all lithological units. The choice of the most appropriate system depends on the specific purpose of the investigation and on the geological characteristics of the study area. In the case of the Belchatów mine, the classification should, obviously, be aimed at a system that would be helpful for developing measures to solve (or, if possible, prevent) engineering-geological and mining problems. © 1994, Elsevier Science B.V. entry.dc:title: Mineralogy and provenance of airborne dust in opencast coal mining areas of South Wales
entry.dc:creator: Merefield J.R.
entry.dc:description: Fugitive dust from opencast mining is a contentious issue. It has often been perceived to be a significant contributor to ambient levels of airborne particulates, even though no reliable means of dust fingerprinting has been available to regulatory authorities. To address this need, dust has been collected continuously for an eighteen month period in and around Ffos Las opencast coal mine in South Wales, over an area covering some 250 square kilometres. It has proven possible for the first time to fingerprint dust from different sources, such as on-site and immediately off-site of the opencast coal workings, and elsewhere in the region. The results show calcite and dolomite to occur over the entire study area, indicating a significant regional component present in airborne dust in the Ffos Las locality. Local sources are recognised by an increase in clay minerals such as chlorite and kaolinite over non-clay minerals such as quartz. Chlorite being detected on-site and occasionally near-site, characterises dust derived from Ffos Las opencast coal workings. -Authors

entry.dc:title: Conservation of mineral nitrogen in restored soils at opencast coal mine sites: II. The effects of inhibition of nitrification and organic amendments on nitrogen losses and soil microbial biomass
entry.dc:creator: WILLIAMSON J.
entry.dc:description: Soils stored in stockpiles during opencast mining operations accumulate significant quantities of ammonium (of the order of 200 μg NH<inf>4</inf><sup>+</sup>‐N g<sup>−1</sup> soil) within the predominantly anaerobic cores of mounds. Upon stockpile dismantling and land restoration, this NH<sup>+</sup><inf>4</inf>‐N is rapidly oxidized to NO<sup>−</sup><inf>3</inf>‐N, which is readily lost from newly restored soil ecosystems by leaching and denitrification. Experiments were set up to examine how these significant reserves of mineral N might be conserved in such situations. Application of the nitrification inhibitor dicyandiamide was successful in minimizing NO<inf>3</inf><sup>−</sup>‐N lost by leaching, though large concentrations of NH<inf>4</inf><sup>+</sup>‐N were detected in drainage waters. Straw incorporation decreased nitrate leaching by up to 40%; biomass C was some 40% greater in straw‐amended than in unamended soils after 14 weeks, though biomass N was similar in both. Addition of nitrogen‐free organic materials (glucose, starch and cellulose) produced different results, with glucose amendment showing the greatest reduction in nitrate leaching in the short term (due to an apparent stimulation of denitrification) whereas addition of cellulose resulted in the most effective conservation of nitrogen over 14 weeks; this was due, at least in part, to uptake of mineral N by the soil microbial biomass. entry.dc:title: The effect of different post‐restoration cropping regimes on some physical properties of a restored soil
entry.dc:creator: Davies R.
entry.dc:description: Abstract. The aggregate stabilities of a soil restored after opencast mining and an undisturbed soil were measured over a complete cropping year from the time of ploughing a grass ley in autumn. This was to examine the effects of various post‐restoration cropping regimes on soil aggregate stability and soil porosity. A wet sieving technique and a mild dispersion method were used to determine indices of soil macro‐ and micro‐aggregate stability, respectively. Air filled porosity at field capacity and crumb porosity were also determined. Removal, storage and restoration decreased macro‐ and micro‐aggregate stability. After restoration, the different grass managements i.e. cutting for silage and grazing, had similar effects on soil aggregate stability and maintained greater aggregate stability than the arable regimes. The pattern of fluctuation in soil macro‐aggregate stability over the year was similar under all crops at both sites, but at the restored site there was a decline in stability, and differences in the air filled porosity at field capacity developed between cropping regimes. Micro‐aggregate stability was less at the restored than at the undisturbed site and showed no seasonal variation or difference between cropping regimes. However, a difference in crumb porosity between cropping regimes did develop. Copyright © 1994, Wiley Blackwell. All rights reserved

entry.dc:title: Selection criteria for the application of continuous mining and transport methods in opencast mines
entry.dc:creator: Kutschera S.
entry.dc:description: Continuous mining and transport methods are gaining increased interest for medium and large size opencast mining operations. This trend is fueled by the fact that belt conveyor systems feature significantly lower operating costs than commonly used truck haulage, especially when applied for high capacity or longer distance transport tasks. This paper highlights some criteria essential for a proper selection of the mining and transport method. It discusses most recent trends in design and application of continuous operating mining and transport equipment. It further compares commonly used methods such as shovel-truck operations with systems comprising continuous operating equipment. Systems such as mobile or semimobile crusher-belt conveyor, bucket wheel excavator round-the-pit-conveyor-spreader, and bucket wheel excavator-cross pit spreader are briefly introduced.

entry.dc:title: Creative conservation and opencast mining
entry.dc:creator: Gough J.
entry.dc:description: Creative conservation was largely a disregarded concept in Britain until the introduction of Town and Country Planning Regulations in 1988. Since then, the applicants and mineral planning authorities together have slowly realized the effects of the Environmental Impact Statement and what is expected of it. Some examples of the implementation of creative conservation in opencast mining are presented.

entry.dc:title: Some trends of problem solving of mineral deposit mining at great depths
entry.dc:creator: Zubkov A.
entry.prism:publicationName: Fiziko Tekhnicheskie Problemy Razrabotki Poleznykh Iskopaemykh
entry.dc:description: Geomechanical situation while mineral deposit mining at great depths with account of regularities of variation of initial depth stresses and three-dimensionality of exhausted strippings is considered. The assumption is drawn on the existence of four mechanisms of rock displacement in the dependence of geological conditions of mineral deposit mining. A variant of combined mining of extended ore bodies is suggested. It is noted, that the study on strength properties of great depth deposits and the strain-stressed state of the open cut structural elements is necessary to conduct while extended ore bodies opencast mining.

entry.dc:title: The Impact of Storage of Soils during Opencast Mining on the Microbial Community: A Strategist Theory Interpretation
entry.dc:creator: Harris J.
entry.dc:description: The microbial community in a soil stripped and stored during opencast coal mining was analyzed. There were significant effects of soil disturbance on the microbial community: in particular, there were large decreases in the total microbial biomass, as determined by ATP analysis, and numbers of fungal propagules as a result of the store construction process, but there was no significant effect on the numbers of bacteria. During the subsequent months of storage there was a flush in the numbers of bacteria, with gram‐negative bacteria showing an increase of nearly 700% in comparison to the control. During this time there was a steady accumulation in the amount of ammonium in the deepest part of the soil store, indicating the onset of anaerobiosis. These changes may be interpreted in terms of lifestyle strategy theory (Grime 1979). The bacteria exhibit behavior typical of R‐strategists, or ruderal species, taking advantage of the nutrients made available by the death of fungal biomass during store construction. Fungi respond as C‐strategists, or competitors, and they are severely affected by store construction‐and unable to persist deep in the anaerobic part of the store. In contrast, anaerobes, S‐strategists or stresstolerators, are able to survive under the same conditions. These changes have serious implications for the restoration of systems using stored topsoil as a resource. The microbial population has been altered in terms of its size and composition. Many of the fungi required for adequate breakdown and incorporation of organic matter will be absent, and the soils will be generally poor in microbial biomass. This will lead to inadequate nutrient cycling and poor soil structural stability, two factors essential for the restoration of a self‐sustaining ecosystem. Copyright © 1993, Wiley Blackwell. entry.dc:title: Land reclamation and restoration of natural ecosystem: A case study from opencast mines of North Eastern Coalfields of India
entry.dc:creator: Singh G.
entry.prism:publicationName: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
entry.dc:description: Coal mining authorities of North Eastern Coalfields have been facing serious challenges of reclamation of the mine lands and restoration of natural ecosystem as a result of opencast mining operations on densely forested hills in Assam. Having regard to present operations, locations of opencast mining and particularly importance of Assam Coal and Its potential use in steel industry and environmental restoration/reclamation measures taken by the NEC authorities, it is justified to continue present opencast mining operations. This case study attempts to present sincere efforts being carried out in environmental restoration by NDC authorities. Background of mining, geology, climate and ecology in the region and also lmpacts of opencast mining operations have been described in this paper. Slope stability and aspects of control of soil wash off are also dealt with particularly civil engineering and mechanical measures such as terracing, bamboo barricading in the slopes, stone-barriers at the toe of dumps, revetment and retaining walls, check-dams in the channels and valleys and gully-plugging etc. Vegetation restoration through plantation of various selected species including turfing/transplantation etc are also presented. Soil quality aspects of in-situ soils dealt with. Vegetation results obtained have been quite successful with survival of diverse species at the rate of over 90%. The aspects of restoration of natural ecosystam restoration in this region of subtropical climate have also been described. © 1993, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

entry.dc:title: Biological reclamation of surface mined land without soil grafting: A working model
entry.dc:creator: Ghosh R.
entry.prism:publicationName: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
entry.dc:description: Opencast mining needs excavation. This, in most cases, mixes the topsoil with subsoil and overburden materials. The excavated mass when occurs in dump, gets washed and losses its topsoil component. Even if any amount is retained, it looses its biolife due to occurring at this displaced place over years. This causes severe loss and hence scarcity of topsoil in mining areas. This, aided by lowering of water table (due to mine water pumping) has caused extensive degraded lands in opencast mining areas. A techno-economically feasible procedure for greening this category of wastelands, without soil grafting has been recommended after thorough field experiment. © 1993, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. entry.dc:title: Determination of the working zone of a dragline bucket - a graphical approach
entry.dc:creator: Pathak K.
entry.dc:description: A dragline is used extensively to remove the overburden in opencast mining operation. The transport efficiency of the dragline depends largely upon the dragging, hoisting and swinging operations with proper bucket suspension. The working zone of the dragline bucket may be determined considering its swinging, dragging and hoisting movement at different planes. In this paper a graphical approach for determination of the bucket path profile of a standard dragline has been indicated considering the simple three period duty cycle in each operation.

entry.dc:title: Prediction of instability of slopes in an opencast mine over old surface and underground workings
entry.dc:creator: Singh T.N.
entry.prism:publicationName: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
entry.dc:description: Jharia coalfield is a chief storehouse of prime coking coal in India, Earlier, many shallow seams were exploited by surface mining but when this method became uneconomical the mine operators resorted to underground method. However, due to various geotechnical problems, it was not possible to fully extract coal by underground method. Opencast mining is now being planned for extraction of coal locked in partially worked coal seam for ensuring maximum recovery. The major problem envisaged in conducting opencast mining in such areas will be the stability of slope. In this paper, the technique adopted for simulation of 144 m thick section of rockmass in equivalent material model is outlined. Old shallow surface excavation upto 33.0 m and later on underground workings were simulated in coal seam II/III. The span of the void was 160 m. An opencast excavation was conducted for recovering locked coal. The behaviour of slopes are reported here. © 1992, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

entry.dc:title: Chances for developments in belt conveyor technology in open pit mines
entry.dc:creator: Hager M.
entry.dc:description: The advantages of belt conveyors for lignite transportation in open pit mines are elucidated. The mobile belt conveyor has proved successful as the only possible system for large mass flows, such as those that are conveyed under the conditions of deep opencast mining. Neither trains nor dumper trucks can be employed in a technically and economically efficient way. Some developments are discussed that have been made in the field of belt conveyor technology outside the mining of lignite, and which could be the starting point for more detailed projects. These include plants with a particularly large conveyor length, particularly large lifting heights and with curved conveying routes.

entry.dc:title: Reliability, production and control in coal mines. Proceedings of an international conference, Wollongong, New South Wales, September 1991
entry.dc:creator: Hargraves A.
entry.prism:publicationName: Reliability Production and Control in Coal Mines Proceedings of an International Conference Wollongong New South Wales September 1991
entry.dc:description: A collection of 64 papers presented at this conference. The only constraint on effective competition between underground mining and opencast mining in Australia is the reliability of underground systems currently at only 40% although individual components reach 95%. entry.dc:title: Effects of subsoiling and associated incorporation of fertilizer on soil rehabilitation after opencast mining for coal
entry.dc:creator: Scullion J.
entry.dc:description: A trial was set up in South Wales in 1980 on land replaced in 1972 after opencast coal mining, to assess the effects on soil rehabilitation of regular subsoiling, through an established sward, with and without incorporation of a ‘semi-organic’ fertilizer into subsoiling slots. Treatments were assessed on the basis of yield, soil structure indices, root and organic contents and earthworm population densities. Apart from yields, data are for the eighth year of the experiment (1987), 18 months after the fourth programme of treatments. Treatments did not markedly affect productivity, although it tended to be higher with subsoiling and fertilizer incorporation. Subsoiling had little effect on root and organic content, but fertilizer incorporation increased the latter, particularly at depth. Earthworm population densities were markedly higher on subsoiled areas, the increase in the deeper burrowing species Aporrectodea caliginosa being largest. Fertilizer incorporation increased abundance of Lumbricus rubellus, but had little effect on other species. Subsoiling reduced surface wetness, but did not result in any significant improvement in structure. Fertilizer incorporation reduced clay dispersion at depth and, with subsoiling, also increased pore space. Treatment responses in term of soil structure were not large, but the incorporation of fertilizer did markedly accelerate structure rehabilitation at depth. Subsoiling alone contributed to land rehabilitation by controlling surface wetness and encouraging an increase in earthworm populations. © 1991, Cambridge University Press. All rights reserved.

entry.dc:title: Alluvial mining in the USSR
entry.dc:creator: Bogdanov E.I.
entry.dc:description: This report concerns continental alluvial placer deposits of precious metals and tin. Alluvial placers constitute the bulk (more than 80%) of the entire stock of genetically different placer deposits prospected in the USSR. More than 40% of these alluvial placer deposits are located in permafrost areas. In the USSR, the main method of alluvial placer mining is that of opencast mining. The bulk of placer gold in the USSR, about 86%, is obtained with methods wherein independent simultaneously operating earthmoving, hauling and processing machines are used. The rest of placer gold output is obtained using dredges. -from Authors

entry.dc:title: Classification and quantification of erosion phenomena, of transport and sedimentation in basins affected by mining in New Caledonia
entry.dc:creator: Danloux J.
entry.dc:description: The topical perturbations (cyclone and multiannual drought) which condition the hydrological regime of New Caledonia rivers and the different phases of opencast mining are compared with the suspended load variations, measured in the Pouembout and Ouenghi catchments. In addition, the analysis of air photography and satellite imagery demonstrates fluvial and coastal geomorphological changes (creation of the Thio meanders, evolution of the Thio and Ouenghi deltas). This study shows that evolution of the exploitation conditions leads to a decreasing number of pollution causes, while alluviation continues. -from English summary

entry.dc:title: The effect of cultivation on structure in soils affected by opencast mining for coal
entry.dc:creator: Scullion J.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture
entry.dc:description: Two grassland sites, reinstated after opencast mining for coal, were used to assess the effect of cultivation on structure rehabilitation. In general, cultivation had an adverse effect over a range of porosity and aggregate stability indices. This effect tended to be more marked in macro‐ rather than micro‐aggregate stability, in the upper rather than the lower half of the tillage layer and at higher intensities of cultivation. Some tillage responses persisted after two years. Cultivation effects were partly explained by mixing of soil within the tilled layer. However, results indicated some direct physical destruction of aggregates and a large reduction in aggregate stability. Data available did not point to any clear cause of this reduction in stability. Nevertheless, there was some evidence that cultivation may have disrupted the stabilisation of aggregates by organic matter, without influencing overall organic content. Net structural responses to cultivation are a balance of adverse and beneficial effects. In replaced soils this balance is negative. For this reason, tillage should be restricted where structure rehabilitation is a priority. Copyright © 1991 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd

entry.dc:title: Ancient copper mining at Wadi Amram, Israel: an archaeological survey
entry.dc:creator: Willies L.
entry.prism:publicationName: Bulletin Peak District Mines Historical Society
entry.dc:description: Extensive underground workings for copper minerals in the soft Kurnub Sandstone (Lower Cretaceous) were examined at three sites. Pottery scatters at surface on Sites 33 and 75 suggest Egyptian New Kingdom workings. At Site 38 similar workings were found, whilst surface and underground pottery and other finds underground suggest the workings were reopened and worked at intervals from the 1st and 2nd to the 7th and 8th centuries AD, with the possibility of further minor working or exploration in late medieval (Mamaluk) times. At site 38, three or four periods of mining, not all necessarily widely spaced in time, were observed. Despite much covering of the original working floors by sand, it was evident that many artefacts remain in place. There is evidence of opencast mining. It is possible to suggest simple beneficiation methods such as hand picking and winnowing appropriate to the ore, though little direct evidence was found. The findings complement previous work done both on mining remains, and particularly on copper smelting in the nearby Timna Valley. -Author

entry.dc:title: Opencast coal production and the planning system
entry.dc:creator: Cromie S.
entry.prism:publicationName: Occasional Papers in Minerals Planning Duncan of Jordanstone College of Art University of Dundee
entry.dc:description: This research concentrated on testing the hypothesis that in relation to mineral resources exploitation, planning authorities were being forced into a "policy vacuum', arising from the conflict between their traditional concern for environmental protection, and the requirement that they should assess the case for "need' on individual opencast mining proposals. The principal methodology employed (outlined in the appendix) centred on a questionnaire survey of selected planning authorities. Following a brief introduction, the author considers the historical development of opencast coal mining, reviews mining authorisation procedures, highlights the planning considerations and the availability of policy and advice, suggests some of the implications for planning authorities, and draws conclusions on the themes emerging from the change in authorisation procedure initiated by the recommendations of the 1981 Flowers Commission. -P.Hardiman

entry.dc:title: UK opencast mining equipment in the 1980’s
entry.dc:creator: Adams J.N.
entry.prism:publicationName: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
entry.dc:description: Opencast coal mining in the UK is currently one of the most profitable mining operations in the world. This level of profitability has been sustained throughout the 1980’s, a decade during which the UK mining Industry has experienced a prolonged strike during 1984 followed by significant internal re-structuring, and operated through a transitional period of planning legislation culminating in the Housing and Planning Act 1986 and Minerals Planning Note 3, May 1988. The summary outlines the background environment of the decade during which time the excavating and haulage equipment being selected by opencast mining contractors has changed significantly to meet the challenge of an increasingly competitive business. © 1990, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC.
